Title: Scalable Thermal Engineering via Femtosecond Laser‐Direct‐Written Phononic Nanostructures
Text:
RESEARCH ARTICLE
www.afm-journal.de
Scalable Thermal Engineering via Femtosecond
Laser-Direct-Written Phononic Nanostructures
Hiroki Hamma, Roman Anufriev, Kazuyoshi Fushinobu,* Masahiro Nomura,*
and Byunggi Kim*
Modern electronics demands innovative thermal management strategy
beyond conventional approaches. Here, A transformative platform bridging
laboratory-scale phononic nanostructures and industrial-scale thermal
engineering is demonstrated via femtosecond laser-induced periodic surface
structures (fs-LIPSS). Laser-direct-written phononic metamaterials is achieved
with throughputs exceeding 10−5 m2 s−1—three orders of magnitude faster
than electron beam lithography—while maintaining nanoscale resolution.
Applied to silicon membranes, the fs-LIPSS reduce thermal conductivity from
101 to 76 W m−1 K−1, surpassing thin-ﬁlm limit predicted by
Fuchs–Sondheimer model. Monte Carlo simulations corroborate these
ﬁndings, showing that long mean free paths are limited by the fs-LIPSS, while
ablation-induced roughness mediates isotropic modulation of thermal
conductivity via enhanced diﬀuse scattering. Thus, this maskless and
resist-free process enables the fabrication of phononic nanostructures that are
CMOS-compatible and scalable to wafer-level dimensions. This work
establishes the fs-LIPSS as a versatile approach that makes phonon
engineering practical for real-world devices, unlocking applications in
quantum technologies, on-chip energy conversion, and high-performance
computing.

1. Introduction
Controlling heat transport is essential for
energy-eﬃcient computing,[1,2] chip-scale
energy conversion,[3–5]
and suppression
of thermal noise in quantum informa-
tion technologies.[6,7] As device dimensions
shrink and power densities increase, mi-
croscopic control of thermal conduction at
the level of phonon, a quantum of lat-
tice vibration, has become a central chal-
lenge in thermal management. Over the
past two decades, the concept of phonon en-
gineering has revealed that heat can be con-
trolled beyond the limits of Fourier’s law
by tailoring the spectral, spatial, and coher-
ence properties of phonons.[8,9] Phononic
nanostructures such as periodic nanohole
arrays demonstrate that dispersion ﬂat-
tening can suppress thermal transport,
while coherent interference eﬀects emerge
at sub-100 nm length scales.[10–12] Experi-
ments in nanostructured semiconductors
have revealed phonon mean free paths
(MFP) spanning from tens of nanome-
ters to microns, conﬁrming that nanos-
tructures within this range can manipu-
late transport through boundary scattering
and ballistic eﬀects.[8,13] These advances establish phononic
nanostructures as promising candidates for nanoscale the-
rmal
insulation,[14]
rectiﬁcation,[15]
and
thermoelectric
conversion.[16,17]
Despite these advances, the lack of scalable fabrication meth-
ods remains a major barrier for practical implementation. Stan-
dard nanostructuring methods, such as electron beam lithogra-
phy (EBL) and focused ion beam (FIB) milling, oﬀer sub-100 nm
resolution for phononic nanostructure fabrication in a maskless
manner. Zhou et al. have demonstrated that the self-assembly of
block copolymers can facilitate phononic crystals and a signiﬁ-
cant reduction in thermal conductivity.[18] However, those con-
ventional methods strongly rely on slow, multi-step, and highly
precise fabrication procedures, limiting high-throughput fabrica-
tion of phononic nanostructures. Nanoimprint lithography has
been proposed as a repeatable approach, yet the fabrication and
maintenance of nanoscale molds remain challenging.[19] As a re-
sult, phononic nanostructures have remained as laboratory-scale
demonstrations, hindering their translation into practical devices
that require wafer-scale integration.

Here, we showcase that femtosecond laser-induced peri-
odic surface structures (fs-LIPSS) can overcome this scalabil-
ity bottleneck by enabling maskless, one-step fabrication of
phononic nanostructures over centimeter-scale regions with
throughputs orders of magnitude higher than electron-beam
lithography. The fs-LIPSS is a laser-direct-writing scheme that
spontaneously produces sub-wavelength periodic ripples on sur-
faces via interference between incident light and surface elec-
tromagnetic waves,[20–22] and has been widely applied for opti-
cal functionalization,[23,24] wettability control,[25–27] tribology,[28,29]
and bioengineering.[30] Applied to single-crystalline silicon thin
ﬁlms, we demonstrate that the fs-LIPSS can reduce the thermal
conductivity signiﬁcantly below the thin-ﬁlm limit predicted by
the Fuchs–Sondheimer (FS) model.[31–33] To elucidate the under-
lying mechanism, we further perform Monte Carlo simulations,
which reveal the role of boundary scattering in the fs-LIPSS. Our
results position the fs-LIPSS as a scalable, CMOS-compatible
platform for phononic thermal engineering, bridging the gap
between fundamental studies of nanoscale heat conduction and
real-world applications.
2. Results and Discussion
2.1. Phononic Nanostructures Fabricated Via fs-LIPSS
The LIPSS are characterized by their spatial frequency relative
to the incident laser. In general, the low-spatial-frequency LIPSS
exhibit a period slightly shorter than the laser wavelength (0.8–
0.9 𝜆laser), while the high spatial frequency LIPSS have periods far
below the laser wavelength (≈0.1 𝜆laser). In this work, we focused
on the low-spatial-frequency LIPSS, as they oﬀer large depth con-
trast with well-deﬁned edges.
For silicon of which bandgap is 1.1 eV, near-infrared wave-
lengths with large optical penetration depths are advantageous
to realize the high-aspect ratio LIPSS. In our experiment, we
scanned the 220-fs laser pulses at 1030 nm (Figure 1a) on a 1-
μm-thick device layer of a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrate to
form the LIPSS. Subsequently, the anisotropic reactive ion etch-
ing (RIE) using sulfur hexaﬂuoride (SF6) and oxygen (O2) under
bias was performed to tune the top silicon thickness (Figure 1b).
This RIE process makes the groove dimension as short as the
phonon MFP, thereby enhancing phonon boundary scattering
(Figure 1c).
Figure 1d,e show the scanning electron microscope (SEM) im-
ages of the fs-LIPSS. The grating structures form perpendicu-
larly to the laser polarization, with a period of 830 nm (0.81
𝜆laser). The inset of Figure 1d shows the 2D fast Fourier trans-
form (2D-FFT) spectrum, where two clear symmetric peaks in
the y-direction conﬁrm the presence of a single well-deﬁned spa-
tial frequency. Cross-sectional SEM image (Figure 1e) reveals that
the RIE shaped the fs-LIPSS rectangular grating structures. The
average neck thickness was 314 nm, which was small enough to
strongly enhance phonon boundary scattering in silicon, whose
bulk phonon MFP spans 100–1,000 nm.[34]
To maximize the regularity of the LIPSS, we optimized laser
irradiation parameters, including ﬂuence and repetition rate.
Figure 2a presents the spatial frequency spectrum along the
dashed line in the inset of Figure 1d. As a ﬁgure of merit, we
used the product of the quality factor (ky, LIPSS/Δky) and the peak
intensity to account for both the dominance of a single frequency
and pattern contrast. For the formation of the regular LIPSS, the
polarization should be ﬁxed perpendicular to the scanning di-
rection, ensuring polarization-perpendicular mode to initiate the
parallel-line ablation along the scanning direction.[35]
Figure 2b shows that the optimum condition was a repeti-
tion rate of 0.5 MHz and a ﬂuence of 1.59 J cm−2. With a 1 e2
spot diameter dspot = 13 μm, the pulse overlap number, deﬁned
by
frdspot
vs , was calculated as 6.5, where vs and fr are the scanning
speed and the repetition rate, respectively. The optimized pulse
overlap number eﬃciently guides the LIPSS growth while pre-
venting excessive ablation. The LIPSS were formed slightly be-
low the uniform ablation threshold. At higher ﬂuences, thermal
and ﬂuid-dynamic instabilities dominate over the interference-
driven periodic ablation, erasing periodicity. At lower ﬂuences,
the periodic heating induces amorphization, leading to only a-
few-nanometers corrugation in height.[36]

further

(Figure 2c). The fs-LIPSS exhibited the sharp silicon peaks
at 520 cm−1, without the peak broadening associated with the
amorphization. Finally, the RIE eﬀectively removed the surface
oxide layer, leaving a monolithic crystalline silicon system.
2.2. Fabrication Throughput Benchmark
To assess the eﬀectiveness of the fs-LIPSS for phononic nanos-
tructuring, we compared their fabrication throughput with rep-
resentative top-down nanofabrication techniques (Figure 3).
Throughput is deﬁned as the processed area per unit time
(m2 s−1), which allows direct comparison across approaches with
diﬀerent mechanisms and resolutions.
FIB oﬀers direct writing capability, but its throughput for 300–
400-nm depth is limited to the order of 10−11–10−9 m2 s−1.[37,38]
EBL provides higher resolution and greater scalability, but still
remains relatively slow, with typical single-beam throughputs of
10−10–10−8 m2 s−1.[39] Recent developments in multibeam EBL
have demonstrated signiﬁcant improvement, reaching the 10−5–
10−4 m2 s−1 regime, though such systems are still at the develop-
ment and pre-commercial stage.[40,41]
Advanced laser-direct-writing techniques based on structured
illumination using a digital micromirror device (DMD) or multi-
beam interference inherently enable parallel patterning. Their
throughputs typically range from 10−7 to 10−4 m2 s−1,[42–44] de-
pending on the projection optics and illuminated area. These
methods oﬀer high speed but require specialized optical setups,
which limit their ﬂexibility and robustness for rapid prototyping
or direct patterning on non-planar substrates.
In contrast, single-beam fs-LIPSS fabrication does not rely on
beam structuring optics, but takes advantage of self-constructed
interference ﬁelds on material surfaces, achieving surprisingly
competitive throughput. Reported values span from 10−6 up to
10−4 m2 s−1, depending on the scan speed and line spacing.[45–48]
For instance, our experimental condition (1 m s−1 scan speed, 9-
μm line spacing) corresponds to 9 × 10−6 m2 s−1, which already
surpasses single-beam EBL by more than three orders of magni-
tude. Notably, high-speed laser scanning, where optimized scan-
ning strategies such as polygon or galvo-based approaches are
employed, has pushed LIPSS throughput into the 10−4 m2 s−1

While not matching the resolution of EBL, the huge advantage

phononic nanostructures. Further investigations to realize ﬁner-

cation route for phonon engineering and thermal management
devices.
2.3. Thermal Conductivity Measurement
The thermal conductivity of the fs-LIPSS was measured us-
ing the micro time-domain thermoreﬂectance (μTDTR) method.
Figure 4a,b show the experimental schematic of the μTDTR and
the SEM image of the sample, respectively. A 10-μs pump pulse
at 488 nm heated up the gold transducer, while a continuous-
wave probe laser at 514 nm monitored the transient temperature
change. To make the measurement solely sensitive to the thermal
conductivity of the fs-LIPSS, we utilized a suspended air bridge
structure of silicon membranes. We changed the orientation of
the fs-LIPSS, which is deﬁned as the angle between the heat dis-
sipation direction and the grooves.
Figure 4c shows representative TDTR curves and their ﬁtting
through the ﬁnite element method (FEM) simulation. The fs-
LIPSS had longer cooling times than the pristine ﬁlm, indicating
reduced eﬀective thermal conductivity. The decay time increased
with increasing orientation angle, as the grating structures

2.4. Monte Carlo Simulation
To further analyze phonon transport, we employed phonon
Monte Carlo simulation (see Methods). Figure 5a shows phonon
ray-tracing results in the fs-LIPSS-like rectangular grating. We in-
jected phonons from the hot side and collected them at the cold
side, enabling the extraction of trajectories and MFP statistics.
Figure 5b,c are phonon scattering angle distributions at the
vertical sidewalls of the fs-LIPSS. Most scattering was diﬀuse fol-
lowing the Lambertian distribution, while the specular scattering
was negligible. The ablation-induced rough surface reduced the
specular scattering probability to nearly zero. Lack of the spec-
ular scattering underlies the absence of phonons guiding and
anisotropy in the LIPSS. For 𝜃= 0° (Figure 5b), scattering was
symmetric, while for 𝜃= 90° (Figure 5c), the back scattering dom-
inated due to the grating geometry perpendicular to the heat ﬂux
direction.

For trench structures with small groove widths like the LIPSS,
the trench width and the neck thickness work synergistically
to manipulate phonon transport. Meanwhile, the MFP cutoﬀ
can be directly related to a laser wavelength (0.81 𝜆laser in the
present context). Considering that long-MFP phonons contribute
signiﬁcantly to thermal conduction, use of shorter wavelength
lasers is required to achieve greater control over phonon trans-
port. For wide-bandgap, high-thermal-conductivity semiconduc-
tors and insulators such as silicon carbide, gallium nitride, and
diamond, the use of visible to UV femtosecond lasers will en-
able dramatic modulation of thermal conductivity for two rea-
sons. First, the large optical penetration depths of those mate-
rials mediate deep ablation depth required for high-aspect ra-
tio LIPSS. Second, the LIPSS period can be signiﬁcantly shorter
than phonon MFP. High-aspect-ratio and short-period LIPSS will
enhance phonon scattering and conﬁnement, potentially mod-
ulate phonon dispersion. In this work, the fs-LIPSS achieved
a neck thickness of 314 nm in silicon, where phonons with
MFP larger than 400 nm contributes 50% of thermal conduc-
tion in its bulk form.[34,59] Huang et al. demonstrated that 300-
fs pulsed with a 520-nm wavelength could be used for fabri-
cation of high-uniformity LIPSS on silicon and 4H silicon car-
bide by manipulating half-periodic mismatched optical enhance-
ment. Further structural control along the thickness direction
could therefore provide an additional route to engineer phonon
transport.
Another promising approach is use of a metallic hard mask
with LIPSS. Metallic materials with short surface-plasmon-
polaritons MFP enable formation of high-uniformity LIPSS.[60]
The uniform structures can be then transferred to the underly-
ing semiconductor or insulator via anisotropic dry etching. This

At cryogenic temperatures, where quasi-ballistic phonon trans-
port becomes prominent, the LIPSS are expected to exhibit
anisotropic thermal conduction and phonon directionality. Since
the LIPSS orientation is inherently determined by the laser po-
larization, this laser-direct-writing scheme oﬀers a unique op-
portunity to encode phonon pathways by on-demand polariza-
tion control. Meanwhile, the surface proﬁle is not perfectly ﬂat
(Figure 1d,e), which may further inﬂuence phonon directionality.
Accordingly, advanced topographic analysis, such as atomic force
microscopy with a high-aspect-ratio cantilever or stereoscopic
SEM, will be necessary for the design of phononic metasurfaces.
With precise control over the LIPSS morphology, it could facili-
tate the construction of phononic circuits, thereby opening new
avenues for integrated phonon-based thermal management.
Beyond these fundamental insights, the LIPSS also provide a
practical advantage in terms of manufacturing processes. This
maskless and resist-free process is compatible with wafer-scale
silicon technology and can be directly integrated into semi-
conductor fabrication workﬂows. More broadly, the scalable
laser-written nanostructures can serve as a versatile platform,
where thermal functionality is combined with additional optical,
electronic, or tribological properties to realize multifunctional
platform.
3. Conclusion
In summary, we have demonstrated that fs-LIPSS oﬀer a simple,
maskless route to fabricate phononic nanostructures directly on
crystalline silicon with a throughput several orders of magnitude
higher than conventional nanolithography techniques. Whereas
electron-beam lithography, focused ion beam, and block copoly-
mer approaches remain indispensable for ultra-high-resolution
patterning, albeit with a low-throughput, fs-LIPSS enable scal-
able nanostructuring over millimeter-scale areas at speeds suit-
able for practical device integration. Crucially, the laser-written
grooves function as eﬀective phononic nanostructures, suppress-
ing thermal conductivity through limitation of long MFP, as
conﬁrmed by the TDTR measurements and Monte Carlo sim-
ulations. Our study establishes the fs-LIPSS as a versatile and
CMOS-compatible platform for large-area thermal management
and phonon engineering, bridging the gap between fundamen-
tal studies of nanoscale heat conduction and scalable device
technologies.
4. Experimental Section
LIPSS Fabrication:
First, we cleaned the SOI wafer using organic sol-
vents (acetone, isopropyl alcohol, and water) in a sonic bath. We utilized
the Galvano scanner (Han’s Scanner, Ultrascan) and f-theta lens to scan
the focused femtosecond laser beam at 1030 nm with 220-fs pulse dura-
tion (EKSPLA, FemtoLux 3). The fabrication was performed under ambient
air conditions (20–22 °C, 30%–45% relative humidity). Before we conduct
the RIE (Figure 1b), we cleaned the surface using acetone in a sonic bath,
to remove ablation residuals.
µTDTR Sample Preparation:
To fabricate the air-bridge sample shown
in Figure 4b, we ﬁrst conducted a photolithography and deposited the 250-
nm-thick gold with a 20-nm-thick chromium adhesion layer by using the
electron beam evaporator, followed by lift-oﬀto form the gold transducer.
Then, the LIPSS was fabricated on the silicon surface as described in the
sub-section LIPSS fabrication. As the gold transducer has larger ablation
threshold than silicon, no mask was required to protect the gold trans-
ducer during the fs-laser scanning. The LIPSS orientation was controlled
by rotating a sample stage. Next, we conducted the second photolithogra-
phy and the RIE to make etching holes. Finally, we suspended the silicon
membrane by removing the silica sacriﬁcial layer with vapor hydroﬂuoric
acid etching through the etching holes.
µTDTR Measurement:
We employed the μTDTR method to measure
the thermal conductivity of the suspended silicon membranes. A 488-nm
pump pulse heated the gold transducer by ≈10 K, while a weak continuous-
wave 514-nm probe laser monitored the resulting transient reﬂectance
change, assuming linear dependence on temperature. Analysis of the tran-
sient temperature decay enabled measurement of the thermal conduc-
tance. Given the density and speciﬁc heat capacity values from literatures
for gold (19,320 kg m−3, 129.7 J kg K)[61] and silicon (2,329 kg m−3, 714
J kg K),[62] the thermal conductivity of the silicon membranes was deter-
mined. We set the thermal conductivity of thin gold as 250 W m K con-
sidering the size eﬀect.[63,64] To extract the material thermal conductiv-
ity considering the periodic nanostructures, we reconstructured the LIPSS
geometry in our FEM simulations. The normalized transient curves were
ﬁtted to the experimental data using least-squares minimization. The 1/e2
diameters of the pump and probe beams were 2.0 and 1.9 μm, respec-
tively. Measurements were repeated on ﬁve identical samples to obtain
statistical standard deviations.
Monte Carlo Simulation:
The MC method has been well established
for simulating thermal conduction in nanostructures.[65–70] We utilized
a FreePATHS simulator.[68–70] In this framework, phonon wave packets
are treated as quasi-particle heat carriers, hereafter referred to simply as
phonons. Phonons propagate along in straight trajectories until they en-
counter scattering events without coherent interference. In our MC simu-
lations, we injected 1000 (Figure 5d,e) or 10 000 (Figure 5a–c) phonons
from hot side in random directions, where their frequencies 𝜔were sam-
pled from Planck’s distribution under the Debye approximation. The group
velocity v was evaluated as d𝜔/dq from the bulk phonon dispersion 𝜔(q),
with the polarization branch assigned randomly. At surface, phonons un-
derwent either specular or diﬀuse boundary scatterings. The probability of
specular scattering p is given as
p = exp
[
−16𝜋2𝜎2cos2 (𝜙)
𝜆2
]
(5)
where 𝜎is the surface roughness, Φ is the incident angle, and 𝜆is the
phonon wavelength. The specular scattering was treated as elastic reﬂec-
tion at surfaces, whereas diﬀuse scattering randomized phonon propaga-
tion directions accoording to the Lambert cosine law.
The MFP for phonon-phonon scattering events was considered as
−ln(r)Λbulk, where r is a random number between zero and one.[68] We as-
sumed Λbulk = 300 nm at 300 K, based on reported literature values.[34,71]
The assumption of a frequency-independent MFP is not ideal, and future
work should incorporate more rigorous frequency-dependent models.
